title: Worked Example 3
summary: Use ΔAPC to find AC, then ΔABC to find AB.
alt: Worked Example 3: In ΔABC, ∠C = 90°. P lies on BC such that BP = 21 cm, PC = 15 cm and AP = 25 cm. Calculate the length of (i) AC, (ii) AB.

hyp.label: Hypotenuse
hyp.text: The side opposite the right angle. It is always the longest side.

legA.label: Shorter side 1
legA.text: One of the two sides that meet at the right angle.

legB.label: Shorter side 2
legB.text: The other side that meets at the right angle.

steps.title: The question
steps.narration: In **ΔABC**, **∠C = 90°**. **P** lies on **BC** such that **BP = 21 cm**, **PC = 15 cm** and **AP = 25 cm**. We have to find (i) **AC** and (ii) **AB**.

steps.title: Spot the right angle
steps.narration: In ΔAPC, **∠C = 90°**, so the **hypotenuse** is the side opposite it: **AP**. The other two sides meet at the right angle. We start with this triangle because two of its sides are known.

steps.title: Pythagoras' theorem
steps.narration: **Pythagoras' theorem**: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{AP^2} &= \role{legA}{PC^2} + \role{legB}{AC^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Make the unknown the subject
steps.narration: We want a **shorter side**, so subtract the known square from the hypotenuse square.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{AP^2} &= \role{legA}{PC^2} + \role{legB}{AC^2} \\ \role{legB}{AC^2} &= \role{hyp}{AP^2} - \role{legA}{PC^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Substitute the lengths
steps.narration: Replace each side by its length.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{AP^2} &= \role{legA}{PC^2} + \role{legB}{AC^2} \\ \role{legB}{AC^2} &= \role{hyp}{AP^2} - \role{legA}{PC^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{25^2} - \role{legA}{15^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Square root
steps.narration: Take the square root of both sides (a length is positive).\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{AP^2} &= \role{legA}{PC^2} + \role{legB}{AC^2} \\ \role{legB}{AC^2} &= \role{hyp}{AP^2} - \role{legA}{PC^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{25^2} - \role{legA}{15^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{625} - \role{legA}{225} \\ &= \role{legB}{400} \\ \role{legB}{AC} &= \sqrt{400} = \role{ans}{20\ \text{cm}}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Add the two parts of BC
steps.narration: To use ΔABC we need the whole side **BC**.\[\begin{aligned}BC &= BP + PC \\ &= 21 + 15 = 36\ \text{cm}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Right angle and theorem
steps.narration: In ΔABC, **∠C = 90°**, so the **hypotenuse** is the side opposite it: **AB**. The other two sides meet at the right angle. **Pythagoras' theorem**: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{AB^2} &= \role{legA}{BC^2} + \role{legB}{AC^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Substitute and add
steps.narration: Put in the lengths, square them and add.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{AB^2} &= \role{legA}{BC^2} + \role{legB}{AC^2} \\ &= \role{legA}{36^2} + \role{legB}{20^2} \\ &= \role{legA}{1296} + \role{legB}{400} \\ &= \role{hyp}{1696}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Square root
steps.narration: 1696 is not a perfect square, so use a calculator and round to 3 significant figures.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{AB^2} &= \role{legA}{BC^2} + \role{legB}{AC^2} \\ &= \role{legA}{36^2} + \role{legB}{20^2} \\ &= \role{legA}{1296} + \role{legB}{400} \\ &= \role{hyp}{1696} \\ \role{hyp}{AB} &= \sqrt{1696} = \role{ans}{41.2\ \text{cm}}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Be careful!
steps.narration: **ΔABP is not right-angled**, so we cannot use Pythagoras' theorem in it directly. Always work through the right-angled triangles in the figure — here **ΔAPC** and then **ΔABC** — one at a time.

formulas.title: Pythagoras' theorem
formulas.text: In a right-angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

formulas.title: Finding the hypotenuse
formulas.text: Add the two squares, then take the square root.

formulas.title: Finding a shorter side
formulas.text: Subtract the known shorter side's square from the hypotenuse's square, then take the square root.

challenges.title: Which triangle?

options.label: ΔAPC — it has a right angle at C
ΔABP — it has the most known sides

challenges.prompt: To find **AC** first, which triangle should we use?
challenges.hint: Look for a triangle that contains the right angle.
challenges.explain: ΔAPC has the right angle at C and two known sides. ΔABP has no right angle, so Pythagoras' theorem cannot be used in it.

takeaways: Pythagoras' theorem works only in **right-angled** triangles — mark every right angle in the figure first.
Split the figure into right-angled triangles and solve them **one at a time**; each answer feeds the next triangle.
Keep a few extra decimal places in the middle of a calculation and round only the **final** answer (3 s.f.).

notes.title: Exam tip
notes.text: Always begin with a line such as "In ΔABC, ∠C = 90°. Using Pythagoras' Theorem," — it shows which triangle and which right angle you are using.

notes.title: Rounding
notes.text: If the answer is not a whole number, give it to **3 significant figures** unless the question says otherwise.
